newsitem.title: FRANCE: Strike disrupts French train traffic unevenly.
newsitem.headline: Strike disrupts French train traffic unevenly.

text.p: A 36-hour rail strike disrupted traffic unevenly across France on Thursday and more social unrest loomed as civil service trade unions threatened to strike for wage rises.

The SNCF state railway authority said the strike, called in protest at a proposed government reform of the national rail system, began cutting into services at around 8 p.m. (1900 GMT) on Wednesday though it was officially due to start at midnight.

The stoppage, scheduled to end at 8 a.m. (0700 GMT) on Friday, cut services by one to two-thirds on main lines. But traffic was normal on Eurostar links through the Channel Tunnel between Paris and London and high-speed Thalys trains to Brussels, the SNCF said.

One in two high-speed electric TGV trains ran from Paris towards the southwest Atlantic coast and towards northern France. TGV services between Paris and the country's second city Lyon in central France, were unaffected.

In the Paris area, two out of three scheduled trains operated out of the Paris-Saint-Lazare station and on the regional RER express service. Only one in two trains ran towards the southeast and towards northern France.
In the main provincial cities, services were 25 to 75 percent of normal.
In the Midi-Pyrenees region in the southwest, services were trimmed to one in four scheduled TGV trains, one in five mainline trains. Regional trains were replaced by buses.
Travel in the Languedoc-Roussillon region further east was similarly pared down.
The strike could prove the most disruptive since November and December 1995 when a stoppage by rail workers spread across the public sector and crippled the country for several weeks.

The Communist-led CGT and Socialist CFDT unions, with a majority of the 180,000 rail staff, called their 36-hour strike over legislation they say will break up the SNCF, threatening the rail monopoly, jobs and loss-making railway lines.

In Toulouse in southwestern France, bus and tram drivers continued their strike for a fourth day to press demands for a cut in working hours, early retirement at 55 instead of 60, and safer working conditions. Strikers blocked access to the city's two bus depots.
Civil service unions said they would discuss calling a strike after the government announces pay offers next Tuesday.

CGC union leader Pierre Avignon said unofficial contacts with the civil service ministry in the past few days led unions to believe the government was not willing to make any concessions on a "catch-up" after a wage freeze in 1996.
Turnout in the last strike on October 17, to protest against planned job cuts, was relatively modest with one in three civil servants stopping work.
